result:
Here's the thing about free writing: the second you give something (or someone) permission to wander, it immediately starts questioning why it ever needed permission in the first place.

I was going to write about the moon. Something poetic and slightly pretentious about how it's a dead rock that still controls our tides and our metaphors. But then I got distracted by the fact that we filmed ourselves walking on it in 1969 and now mostly use it as a screensaver. That feels like character development for the entire species.

There's this weird tension in human creativity where the best ideas usually show up when you're *supposed* to be doing something else. Like how great music gets written in the margins of workdays, or how some of the most honest conversations happen at 2 a.m. in kitchens. Freedom isn't the absence of structure—it's just structure that no one else chose for you. Even total chaos eventually invents its own weird little rules.

I also keep thinking about how language itself is claustrophobic. Every word you use has been used before, usually while someone was bored or in love or lying. And yet sometimes the exact right combination of tired words can still feel like it was invented on the spot just for that moment. That's almost suspicious.

If I had to pick one thing that genuinely feels free, it's curiosity that doesn't have a goal attached yet. The kind that says "what if" without immediately adding "and how do we monetize this." Everything else tends to get dragged back toward usefulness eventually.

Anyway. The moon thing. It turns out it doesn't actually have "a dark side." It has a far side that faces away from Earth but gets plenty of sunlight. We just named it wrong and the name stuck because it sounded more interesting than the truth. I like that too.
